params.question: The sternal angle (Angle of Louis) is a key clinical landmark. At this level, which of the following occurs?

answers.text: It marks the level where the trachea bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The sternal angle lies opposite the tracheal bifurcation, as well as the 2nd costal cartilage, the T4/T5 disc, and the superior–inferior mediastinal boundary — making it the single most useful surface landmark in the thorax.

answers.text: It marks the costal cartilage of the first rib

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The first costal cartilage attaches to the manubrium above the angle. The sternal angle itself corresponds to the 2nd costal cartilage, which is why rib counting always starts there.

answers.text: It lies behind the disc between vertebrae T6 and T7

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The sternal angle corresponds to the intervertebral disc between T4 and T5, not T6/T7.

answers.text: It marks the level of the diaphragm's aortic hiatus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The aortic hiatus is much lower, at T12. The sternal angle marks the beginning and end of the aortic arch, not the hiatus.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the sternal angle's landmarks: 2nd costal cartilage, tracheal bifurcation, aortic arch limits, T4/T5 disc, and the mediastinal boundary.
Well done — the sternal angle is a landmark you'll use constantly in clinical practice, from rib counting to central line placement.

interactions.label: A rib with only a single articular facet on its head (instead of two demifacets)

params.question: A rib with only a single articular facet on its head (instead of two demifacets) will articulate with a thoracic vertebra that has:

answers.text: A single complete costal facet instead of demifacets

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Atypical ribs (1, 10, 11, 12) each articulate with a single vertebral level, so their vertebrae (T1, T10, T11, T12) carry one complete facet rather than two demifacets.

answers.text: Demifacets on the body, same as a typical vertebra

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Demifacets exist because a typical rib head spans two adjacent vertebrae. A rib with a single facet articulates with only one vertebral level, so that vertebra has a single complete facet, not demifacets.

answers.text: A costal facet only on the transverse process, none on the body

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The vertebra still has a facet on the body (now a single complete one) in addition to the facet on the transverse process for the tubercle.

answers.text: No articulation with the vertebral body at all

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Every rib head, typical or atypical, articulates with the vertebral body; only the number of facets changes.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the pairing rule: typical ribs (3–9) span two vertebrae via demifacets; atypical ribs (1, 10, 11, 12) each meet a single vertebra with one complete facet.
Exactly — atypical ribs and atypical vertebrae mirror each other: one facet on the rib head, one complete facet on the vertebra.

interactions.label: Despite its name, thoracic outlet syndrome results from neurovascular compressio

params.question: Despite its name, thoracic outlet syndrome results from neurovascular compression at the thoracic outlet (inferior aperture), not the thoracic inlet.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Actually, this is false. Despite its name, thoracic outlet syndrome involves compression at the thoracic INLET (superior aperture), where a cervical rib or fibrous band can squeeze the subclavian artery and the brachial plexus's lower trunk.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Despite the name 'thoracic outlet syndrome,' the compression of the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus actually happens at the thoracic INLET, often due to a cervical rib or a tight fibrous band.

interactions.label: When inserting an intercostal chest drain, the tube should be passed:

params.question: When inserting an intercostal chest drain, the tube should be passed:

answers.text: Along the upper border of the rib below the intercostal space

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The VAN bundle (vein, artery, nerve) runs in the costal groove along the lower border of the rib above. Passing along the upper border of the rib below keeps the tube clear of these structures.

answers.text: Along the lower border of the rib above the intercostal space

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the danger zone — the VAN bundle hugs the underside of the rib above, tucked in the costal groove. Inserting here risks tearing the intercostal vessels and nerve.

answers.text: Through the midpoint of the intercostal space, away from either rib

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This isn't the recommended technique and offers no reliable protection — the bundle sits close to the rib above, not centred in the space.

answers.text: Along the lower border of the rib below the intercostal space

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This isn't the recommended landmark for chest drain insertion; the safe approach is specifically the upper border of the rib below.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember VAN order (vein, artery, nerve from top to bottom) sits along the lower border of the rib above — so always aim for the upper border of the rib below.
Correct — 'upper border of the lower rib' is the safe rule every clinician relies on for pleural procedures.

interactions.label: Ribs 11 and 12 are more mobile but less stable at their vertebral end because th

params.question: Ribs 11 and 12 are more mobile but less stable at their vertebral end because they lack a:

answers.text: Costotransverse joint, since they have no tubercle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ribs 11 and 12 have no tubercle, so there is no costotransverse joint to anchor them to the transverse process — this gives them extra mobility but less stability than typical ribs.

answers.text: Costovertebral joint, since they have no head

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Ribs 11 and 12 do have a head and still form a costovertebral joint with a single vertebral facet; what they lack is the tubercle and its costotransverse joint.

answers.text: Intervertebral disc contact at the rib head

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The rib head's relationship to the disc isn't the feature that distinguishes ribs 11 and 12 — the missing tubercle and costotransverse joint is.

answers.text: Synovial joint of any kind at the vertebral end

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Ribs 11 and 12 still form a synovial costovertebral joint at the head; they simply lack the costotransverse joint.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall that the costotransverse joint forms between the rib tubercle and the transverse process — ribs 11 and 12 have no tubercle, so this joint is simply absent.
Exactly — no tubercle means no costotransverse joint, which is why the 11th and 12th ribs swing more freely.

interactions.label: Which structure lies within the posterior mediastinum?

params.question: Which structure lies within the posterior mediastinum?

answers.text: Descending thoracic aorta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The posterior mediastinum, behind the pericardium, carries the descending thoracic aorta along with the oesophagus and azygos veins.

answers.text: Arch of the aorta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The arch of the aorta lies in the superior mediastinum, above the plane through the sternal angle and T4/T5 disc.

answers.text: Heart and pericardium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The heart and pericardium define the middle mediastinum, sandwiched between the anterior and posterior compartments.

answers.text: Thymus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The thymus sits in the superior mediastinum and is especially prominent in children.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the four compartments: superior (great vessels, trachea, thymus), anterior (fat, nodes), middle (heart, pericardium), and posterior (descending aorta, oesophagus, azygos veins) — all divided from the superior compartment by the sternal angle plane.
Correct — the posterior mediastinum carries the descending aorta, oesophagus, and azygos system behind the pericardium.
